questions.prompt: What does the Single Responsibility Principle state?

options.text: A class or module should have only one reason to change.
options.explanation: SRP states that a module should serve only one cohesive purpose.

options.text: A Swift file must contain only one function definition.
options.explanation: SRP does not restrict a class to having only one function.

options.text: Every iOS screen must use a single view controller class.
options.explanation: Using multiple child view controllers is recommended in iOS.

options.text: An application can only run on a single hardware processor core.
options.explanation: SRP is an architecture principle, not hardware thread assignment.

questions.prompt: What does the Open/Closed Principle recommend when adding new functionality?

options.text: Always delete existing code before writing replacement logic.
options.explanation: Deleting existing working code risks regressions and breaks tests.

options.text: Extend behavior by adding new types rather than modifying working code.
options.explanation: OCP says code should be open for extension but closed for modification.

options.text: Never write new Swift classes after the first app release.
options.explanation: OCP encourages writing new conforming types to add features.

options.text: Wrap all database tables inside open access control blocks.
options.explanation: Access control keywords are distinct from the Open/Closed Principle.

questions.prompt: What is the core rule of the Liskov Substitution Principle?

options.text: Subclasses must always override every method in the parent class.
options.explanation: Overriding every method is not required by Liskov Substitution.

options.text: Structs must always be converted into reference classes before use.
options.explanation: Liskov Substitution applies to subtypes, not struct conversions.

options.text: Subtypes must be substitutable for base types without breaking code.
options.explanation: A subtype must preserve the behavioral contracts of its parent type.

options.text: Functions must return values of the exact same size in bytes.
options.explanation: LSP concerns behavioral substitutability, not byte sizes.

questions.prompt: Why does the Interface Segregation Principle advise writing small protocols?

options.text: Because Xcode crashes when protocols have more than four methods.
options.explanation: Xcode compiles protocols of any reasonable size without crashing.

options.text: Because Swift structs cannot conform to protocols with five methods.
options.explanation: Swift structs can conform to protocols with any number of methods.

options.text: Because smaller protocols reduce total compiled app binary size by half.
options.explanation: Protocol count has negligible impact on compiled binary size.

options.text: So types are not forced to implement methods they do not need.
options.explanation: ISP keeps interfaces focused so conforming types avoid dummy stubs.

questions.prompt: What does the Dependency Inversion Principle require high-level modules to do?

options.text: Depend on abstractions like protocols rather than concrete classes.
options.explanation: DIP states high-level modules must depend on abstractions.

options.text: Instantiate all dependencies directly inside their initializers.
options.explanation: Instantiating concrete dependencies creates tight coupling.

options.text: Execute all network requests on background thread queues only.
options.explanation: Threading is an execution detail, not dependency inversion.

options.text: Store all configuration variables inside the device UserDefaults.
options.explanation: UserDefaults is persistence, not dependency inversion architecture.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between Dependency Inversion and Dependency Injection?

options.text: They are identical terms with the exact same meaning in Swift.
options.explanation: One is an architectural principle; the other is a technique.

options.text: Inversion is the principle; Injection is the technique to pass them.
options.explanation: Dependency Inversion is the rule; Dependency Injection passes objects in.

options.text: Inversion is for structs, while Injection is exclusively for classes.
options.explanation: Both concepts apply equally to structs, classes, and actors.

options.text: Inversion was deprecated by Apple in favor of Combine publishers.
options.explanation: Dependency Inversion remains a foundational software principle.

questions.prompt: Which code structure frequently violates the Open/Closed Principle when adding features?

options.text: A struct conforming to a protocol using an extension block.
options.explanation: Using protocols and extensions follows OCP cleanly.

options.text: An actor isolating access to an array of cached records.
options.explanation: Actors manage data race safety, not OCP violations.

options.text: A giant switch statement modified every time a new case arrives.
options.explanation: Adding cases to existing switch statements modifies working code.

options.text: A generic function operating on any Numeric conforming type.
options.explanation: Generics are open for extension by nature.

questions.prompt: What is an example of violating the Liskov Substitution Principle in Swift?

options.text: A struct adopting two protocols using protocol composition.
options.explanation: Protocol composition is standard Swift practice.

options.text: A subclass adding a new property with a default integer value.
options.explanation: Adding properties does not break parent class contracts.

options.text: An extension implementing a computed property on a model struct.
options.explanation: Computed properties do not violate substitution rules.

options.text: A subclass overriding a save method to trigger a fatalError crash.
options.explanation: Throwing fatalError where the parent succeeded breaks substitution.

questions.prompt: How does Swift protocol composition support the Interface Segregation Principle?

options.text: It lets clients combine focused protocols with the ampersand operator.
options.explanation: Swift allows combining small protocols like Readable & Writable easily.

options.text: It forces every protocol method to have an empty default body.
options.explanation: Default bodies are optional extensions, not protocol composition.

options.text: It converts all protocol requirements into objective-c selectors.
options.explanation: Protocol composition is pure Swift syntax.

options.text: It removes the need for type safety checks during compilation.
options.explanation: The compiler strictly type checks protocol composition.

questions.prompt: Does the Single Responsibility Principle mean a class may only contain one method?

options.text: Yes, classes with two or more methods violate clean code rules.
options.explanation: A class can have multiple methods serving the same responsibility.

options.text: No, it means a class should serve one cohesive actor or purpose.
options.explanation: Cohesive responsibilities can span multiple related methods.

options.text: Yes, unless the class conforms to the Swift Sendable protocol.
options.explanation: Sendable manages concurrency, not method count limits.

options.text: No, it only applies to functions that accept closure arguments.
options.explanation: SRP applies broadly to modules, classes, structs, and actors.

questions.prompt: How does Dependency Inversion help reduce unit test execution time?

options.text: It disables the Xcode compiler optimizations during build phases.
options.explanation: Compiler optimizations are controlled by Xcode build settings.

options.text: It compresses the test binary files using gzip compression algorithms.
options.explanation: Binary compression does not speed up test execution.

options.text: It allows passing fast in-memory mocks instead of waiting on networks.
options.explanation: Mock objects run in memory in milliseconds without network latency.

options.text: It runs all test cases directly on the GPU shader pipeline cores.
options.explanation: Unit tests execute on CPU cores.

questions.prompt: What risk arises from over-applying the Interface Segregation Principle?

options.text: Memory leaks caused by weak protocol property conversions.
options.explanation: Protocols do not cause memory leaks on their own.

options.text: The Swift compiler disabling ARC for all conforming types.
options.explanation: ARC operates regardless of protocol count.

options.text: Runtime crashes caused by protocol buffer stack overflows.
options.explanation: Protocols in Swift do not trigger buffer stack overflows.

options.text: Protocol explosion, creating confusing single-method interfaces.
options.explanation: Over-fragmenting protocols causes clutter and excessive boilerplate.

questions.prompt: How does the Single Responsibility Principle relate to UIKit view controllers?

options.text: It encourages moving networking and persistence out of the controller.
options.explanation: Moving non-UI tasks to services prevents Massive View Controllers.

options.text: It requires all table cells to be defined inside the view controller.
options.explanation: Cells should be separate reusable classes, not in the controller.

options.text: It forbids using navigation controllers inside iOS applications.
options.explanation: Navigation controllers are standard UIKit containers.

options.text: It demands that all model validation runs in the storyboard file.
options.explanation: Storyboards define UI elements, not validation logic.

questions.prompt: Which SOLID principle is most directly violated by a fat protocol containing twenty methods?

options.text: The Single Responsibility Principle.
options.explanation: While related, protocol method bloat is the core target of ISP.

options.text: The Interface Segregation Principle.
options.explanation: ISP explicitly addresses fat interfaces that force dummy implementations.

options.text: The Liskov Substitution Principle.
options.explanation: LSP addresses subtype substitutability, not interface size.

options.text: The Open/Closed Principle.
options.explanation: OCP addresses extensibility without modification.

questions.prompt: Why does Swift favor protocol-oriented composition over deep class inheritance?

options.text: Because Swift classes cannot inherit from other Swift classes.
options.explanation: Swift classes support single inheritance.

options.text: Because class inheritance disables memory safety checks in Xcode.
options.explanation: Inheritance maintains full memory safety under ARC.

options.text: Because composition avoids fragile base classes and LSP violations.
options.explanation: Composition allows flexible reuse without deep brittle class hierarchies.

options.text: Because protocols execute four times faster than virtual methods.
options.explanation: Protocol witness tables have similar overhead to class vtables.

questions.prompt: Summarize the five SOLID principles and explain what each letter stands for.

rubric.criterion: Lists all 5 principles: Single Responsibility, Open/Closed, Liskov Substitution, Interface Segregation, and Dependency Inversion.
Accurately defines the core rule of each principle in plain English.

questions.modelAnswer:
The five SOLID principles are:

1. S — Single Responsibility Principle: A class or module should have only one reason to change.
2. O — Open/Closed Principle: Software entities should be open for extension, but closed for modification.
3. L — Liskov Substitution Principle: Subtypes must be substitutable for their base types without breaking application correctness.
4. I — Interface Segregation Principle: Clients should not be forced to depend on methods they do not use; prefer small protocols.
5. D — Dependency Inversion Principle: High-level modules should depend on abstractions like protocols rather than concrete classes.

questions.prompt: How does the Open/Closed Principle help prevent bugs when adding a new payment method to an iOS checkout system?

rubric.criterion: Contrasts modifying existing switch statements (which risks regressions in tested code) with creating new conforming types.
Explains how a shared PaymentMethod protocol allows the checkout service to accept new payment providers without changing its implementation.

questions.modelAnswer:
Without the Open/Closed Principle, adding a new payment method requires opening the existing CheckoutService and adding a new case to a growing switch statement. This creates regression risk because editing working code can accidentally break existing, tested payment methods.

With the Open/Closed Principle, we define a PaymentMethod protocol with a pay(amount:) method. When adding Apple Pay or Klarna, we write a completely new struct conforming to PaymentMethod. The CheckoutService remains closed to modification because it interacts solely through the protocol. It handles the new method without changing a single line of existing code.

questions.prompt: What is the Liskov Substitution Principle, and what is a common way iOS developers violate it?

rubric.criterion: Defines Liskov Substitution: any subclass or conforming type must fulfill the parent contract without breaking correctness.
Provides a common violation: subclassing a type and overriding a method with fatalError or empty no-op because the subclass cannot support it.

questions.modelAnswer:
The Liskov Substitution Principle states that objects of a superclass should be replaceable with objects of its subclasses without breaking program correctness.

A frequent violation in iOS occurs when a developer subclasses a type but cannot support all of its methods. For example, creating a ReadOnlyFile subclass of File, where the save() method is overridden with fatalError("Cannot write"). Code expecting a File instance will crash when passed the subclass. To avoid this, developers should use protocols and composition (such as Readable and Writable) instead of forced class inheritance.

questions.prompt: Explain how the Dependency Inversion Principle enables fast, reliable unit testing in an iOS app.

rubric.criterion: Explains that high-level modules like ViewModels depend on protocol abstractions rather than concrete network or database classes.
Explains that tests inject mock implementations via initializers, enabling fast in-memory testing without network latency or server dependencies.

questions.modelAnswer:
The Dependency Inversion Principle states that high-level modules should depend on abstractions like protocols rather than concrete classes.

In iOS apps, a ViewModel should not instantiate URLSession or a real database directly. Instead, it accepts a protocol like UserLoader in its initializer. In production, the app passes a real network loader. In unit test targets, the test passes a MockUserLoader.

This mock returns predefined data instantly in memory. Tests run in milliseconds, avoid network timeouts, and test edge cases like error responses reliably without relying on live backend servers.

questions.prompt: What is the Interface Segregation Principle, and how does Swift protocol composition make it easy to follow?

rubric.criterion: Defines Interface Segregation: clients should not be forced to depend on methods they do not use, favoring small protocols.
Explains that Swift allows composing small protocols using the ampersand operator (&) so types can adopt multiple focused capabilities.

questions.modelAnswer:
The Interface Segregation Principle states that clients should not be forced to depend on interfaces they do not use. Instead of one large protocol with dozens of methods, developers should create small, focused protocols.

Swift makes this principle natural through protocol composition. Developers define small protocols like Readable, Writable, and Resetable. A simple component can conform only to Readable without writing dummy stubs for write. When a class requires multiple capabilities, Swift combines them cleanly using the ampersand operator, such as Readable & Writable.
